name: Etherington Qualifies Reduced Action Intensity Through Peer Discussion
text: Etherington and colleagues qualify Kaal's exploratory result. In a multicenter vignette study, internal medicine residents first decided alone and then deliberated in small peer groups. Discussion reduced practice intensity and increased clinical certainty beyond the result expected from averaging individual scores. Practice intensity meant willingness to order tests, consultations, or treatment. That result offers narrow evidence that discussion can lower action intensity through interaction. Still, the correspondence does not establish better decisions. The instrument did not measure whether less intense practice was appropriate, and the study did not examine autonomous agents or work-product approval. It also provides no evidence on unanimity, net discrimination, or Kaal's reported effects.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: In this multicenter, vignette-based study of resident PI, we found that working in peer groups reduced PI and increased CC more than would be expected from averaging group members' individual scores.
These findings suggest that coming to an answer as a group was not a matter of compromising to the middle, but instead that discussing the cases moved the whole group toward less intense practice.
It is not designed to measure the appropriateness of more or less intense practice, which is an important question worthy of further investigation.
